Great product.
Real engineering problems underneath it worth knowing before you connect your live data.
but here are few problems I found reading the playbook closely:
No audit trail on agent writes. When an agent updates your CRM stage from a misread email, you need to know what changed, why, and what the value was before. There is no described mechanism for this.
!!!Prompt injection through email. Connecting your inbox directly to a CRM-writing agent is a documented attack surface. Greshake et. in (2023) demonstrated that instructions embedded in received emails can manipulate agents into corrupting your own data. The playbook connects exactly this pipeline.
No operational ceiling on scheduled agents. Agents that run on a schedule with no described limit.
multi-agent race conditions. The inbox triage agent and daily brief agent both hit the same task database. No concurrency control is described. Last write wins, silently.
!GDPR obligations has no rollout plan.
None of this means do not use it. The idea is right. But there is a gap between a compelling demo and a governed system running on production data. Small businesses following this plan will be on the wrong side of that gap without knowing it.

Can't afford a top-tier security suite? Here is how to match its effectiveness:
Instructions
+Install Comodo Free Firewall and activate all its shields; the firewall module must be set to "Safe Mode."
+Update Windows Defender and enable ransomware and exploit protection.
+Use a next-gen VPN ---> https://bit.ly/4pGC1qe
At that URL, request your "vpn.conf" file featuring rate limiting, raw IP, secure DNS, and a kill switch—"FREE and SECURE."
+Watch the tutorial ---> https://bit.ly/4fsvv1q
+Download a WireGuard client such as WireSock or WireGuard (both are recommended).
+Use browser security extensions from providers like Bitdefender, Malwarebytes, Symantec, Avast, Windows Defender, or Emsisoft.
+Scan your devices (mobile, desktop) for malware.
+Avoid using removable drives at work, as worms spread easily that way.
+Upgrade your Wi-Fi router to Wi-Fi 6 or 7 with built-in antivirus features (e.g., ASUS, TP-Link, WatchGuard, or FortiAP).

Put agents on the rest"? This is precisely why billions are currently being poured into a leaking bucket.
The idea that you can completely cut humans out of the equation and let autonomous agents run your business, relationships, and outputs under the illusion that they will magically build trust on the first try is the biggest delusion of our time.
Technology is already exceptionally advanced. Continuing this blind chase for full autonomy and the replacement of human judgment makes zero sense.
* You cannot build a one-dollar transaction on an agent.
* A script will never close a billion-dollar acquisition.
* And trust—whether in business or in life—can never be automated.
A machine has no conscience or responsibility. Its output will always be a pure reflection of the human holding the reins.
Stop outsourcing human judgment and turning people into extras in their own companies. Let's build systems where technology amplifies human intelligence, but **ultimate responsibility and trust always stay in human hands.**
You can automate processes. You can never automate trust.

A playbook may help someone use a tool.
My books are not playbooks for using AI apps.
They are about the deeper conditions underneath failure, readiness, judgment, and consequence.
The Invisible Signals of Failure is about why strong systems fail while still looking strong. It explains how failure forms before it becomes visible, and why leaders often miss truth until damage is already moving.
The Agentic Risk is about AI that acts. It looks at agents, automation, delegated authority, tool use, and why AI that can take action will test organizations faster than AI that only answers.
The Human Margin is about protecting human strength, judgment, kindness, and capacity in a faster, more automated world. It is about what organizations lose when speed, efficiency, and control leave people with no room to think, recover, or challenge.
All three are available on Amazon under Donald P Andrechek.
They are connected by the same question:
Can the system still see truth, manage tempo, prepare before reliance, and protect Capacity Margin before consequence attaches?
That is not a Notion guide.
That is the work underneath the tools.

CODITECT surrounds your existing AI developers and agent fleets with a vendor-agnostic control plane. We don't replace your models or your IDEs—we wrap them to deliver absolute, auditable visibility.

Donald A. 3rd+Donald A. • 3rd+

Author | Inventor of TTP | AI Readiness, Agentic Risk & System Failure Frameworks

2w

Attila Elek Capturing every code change matters.
Signed evidence matters.
A structural diff matters.
Auditability matters.
But proof that a change happened is not the same as proof that the change should have happened.
That is where many control planes stop too early.
The harder questions are upstream.
Who authorized the agent to make the change?
What requirement or risk condition justified it?
What did the agent rely on?
What human reviewed the intent?
What consequence could the code change create?
What should have triggered refusal, rollback, or escalation?
This is where TTP applies.
Truth asks whether the certificate reflects the real decision context, not only the technical delta.
Tempo asks whether developer velocity is moving faster than judgment.
Preparation asks whether refusal, rollback, review, and recovery were tested before agentic coding scaled.
Capacity Margin asks whether security, engineering, audit, and leadership have enough room to challenge the change before it becomes production risk.
Verifiable proof is important.
But enterprise trust depends on proving both what changed and why the system was allowed to change it.

"Put agents on the rest" is a fantastic productivity pitch, but it's a terrifying legal strategy for any business operating in Europe.

As a Compliance Architect navigating the EU AI Act, I see companies following these playbooks to connect autonomous agents to their live data, completely unaware that delegating work also delegates legal liability.

Under Article 10, if an agent mismanages client data or triggers a high-risk failure, regulators won't accept "it was in our workspace" as an excuse. They demand cryptographic proof of the agent's reasoning.
If your operations aren't anchored to a High-Density Forensic Ledger (HDFL), you aren't scaling productivity; you're scaling un-auditable risk.
Productivity tools help you move fast.
Cryptographic governance ensures you survive the audit when an agent moves too fast.

Donald A. 3rd+Donald A. • 3rd+

Author | Inventor of TTP | AI Readiness, Agentic Risk & System Failure Frameworks

2w

Follow

Ioan Ciprian Popa Agentic AI does create a serious evidence problem.
When an agent touches live data, invokes tools, changes records, or triggers workflows, the organization needs proof of what happened, what was authorized, what evidence was relied on, and who remained accountable.
But that is not the same as saying Article 10 requires cryptographic proof of an agent’s reasoning.
Article 10 is mainly about data and data governance for high risk AI systems.
The stronger point is this:
Organizations need defensible evidence before, during, and after agentic action.
That is where TTP applies.
Truth asks whether the record reflects real authority, evidence, and data conditions.
Tempo asks whether agentic action is moving faster than review can keep up.
Preparation asks whether logging, refusal, rollback, and escalation were tested before deployment.
Capacity Margin asks whether people have enough room to challenge the agent before the record becomes damage.
Cryptographic evidence may help.
But governance should not be sold by overstating the law.
The real issue is proving what the agent was allowed to do and why.

I agree with this and many of the comments. The key is to protect core systems of record - ringfenced with rules and well controlled security access. Expand that platform by connecting other systems of record using authenticated connectors that support your process workflows, bolt on controlled AI user interfaces / agents and chatbots that are trained on your systems of record to improve some of the quality and efficiency of the workflows - this is the organic steps many platform developers are taking to incorporate AI into their platforms and these are positive steps (although more enhancing jobs than directly replacing them as a human-in-the-loop is still critical).

However - users want AI engines such as Copilot and Claude, expecting a response grounded on your data and truly interact with platform content / flows. But ... the real trick is to connect up using an MCP connector with pre-defined skills.md that provide the guard rails and set the rules of engagement. The MCP connector respects the platforms structure, privileges and exposes the tools and data you permit in a controlled way. The skills influence the AI behaviour - then it is over to the user - it's still the wild west - but "fill your boots!" as the saying goes.

Jolyon Grace A system of record is not automatically a source of truth. It can contain stale, incomplete, disputed, or poorly governed data. Ringfencing it protects access, not accuracy or legitimacy.
MCP is also a connection protocol, not a governance control. It can expose permitted tools and data, but it does not prove that permissions are appropriate, that tool combinations are safe, or that an action remains legitimate when context changes.
A skills file may influence behaviour. It does not enforce behaviour. Instructions can be misapplied, overridden, conflicted, or bypassed through tool interactions.
The human-in-the-loop claim is equally weak. A human may remain present after AI has already selected evidence, narrowed options, and framed the decision.
TTP tests what the architecture misses: whether truth remains intact, tempo stays within reach of judgment, preparation was proven before reliance formed, and Capacity Margin still exists to challenge, stop, verify, and recover.
“Fill your boots” is precisely the wrong conclusion after describing a controlled environment.

Truth asks what the work is really doing.
Tempo asks whether speed is hiding poor design.
Preparation asks whether the process deserves reliance.
Capacity Margin asks whether people have room to challenge work that should no longer exist.

In strategy and content, the real test is whether the work remains original, accurate, defensible, and connected to human judgment. Faster production means little if the thinking becomes generic, the evidence weakens, or the system begins shaping conclusions people no longer challenge.
AI can support work, but it should never be confused with authorship, judgment, or strategy itself. Those remain human responsibilities.
TTP asks whether truth can still reach the decision, whether tempo is outrunning judgment, whether preparation was proven before reliance formed, and whether people retain enough Capacity Margin to question, verify, and correct.
The goal is not simply to move faster. It is to ensure the work remains worth trusting.

Corey Tate The more important question is not how teams are using AI to move faster. It is whether speed is improving the work or quietly weakening the thinking underneath it.
In strategy and content, AI can produce polished language long before the evidence, originality, judgment, or accountability is strong enough to support it. A piece can sound sharp while the reasoning has become thinner and the human voice less distinct.
TTP tests those conditions. Truth asks whether the work remains connected to reality and evidence. Tempo asks whether production speed is outrunning judgment. Preparation asks whether the people, sources, and review process were ready before reliance formed. Capacity Margin asks whether there is still enough room to question, verify, revise, and reject what appears convincing.
This is central to The Human Margin and The Invisible Signals of Failure. The goal is not faster content. It is work that remains original, defensible, and worth trusting.

Etopian Systems Corp. I appreciate the recognition, but one correction matters: TTP is not a checkpoint teams simply pass before moving ahead.
Capacity Margin is the operating room people and systems retain when conditions become uncertain. It includes time to think, authority to stop, access to evidence, staffing depth, recovery options, and protection for those who challenge the direction.
When that margin disappears, a human may still be “in the loop” while having no practical ability to verify, refuse, or correct anything. Oversight then becomes symbolic.
Speed is not inherently the problem. The problem begins when Tempo outruns judgment, Truth is filtered, Preparation is assumed, and Capacity Margin has already been consumed.
That is why AI transformation cannot be judged by adoption, output, or speed alone. The real test is whether the organization still has enough room to detect error and change course before consequence attaches.
Corey Tate, how do you see organizations proving that margin is real rather than merely claimed?
